# Real analysis {#sec-real-analysis}

Real analysis is the theory behind calculus: what a limit is, when an infinite sum has a value, what it means for
a function to be continuous, differentiable or integrable, and how these notions extend to functions of several
variables. This chapter develops it in six sections, each on explicit examples. Real numbers, sequences and limits
fixes the completeness of the real line and the vocabulary of limits, Cauchy sequences and monotone convergence.
Series treats infinite sums, absolute convergence, the convergence tests and power series with their radius of
convergence. Continuity and differentiability defines limits of functions, continuity, the derivative, and the
mean value and Taylor theorems. The Riemann integral defines the integral as a limit of sums, proves the
fundamental theorem of calculus and treats improper integrals, with the Gaussian integral as the central example.
Calculus on $\mathbb{R}^n$ extends derivatives to several variables, with the Jacobian matrix, the chain rule and
the inverse function theorem. Multiple integrals and convergence of functions ends with the change of variables
formula, uniform convergence and differentiation under the integral sign. Every statement is followed by three
examples of increasing complexity and three exercises of increasing difficulty with hidden solutions. The reader
who knows this material can skim the definitions and try the exercises; the
sequences $1/n$, $(1 + 1/n)^n$, the geometric and harmonic series, the exponential function and the Gaussian
$e^{-x^2}$ are the running examples.

## Real numbers, sequences and limits {#sec-sequences-limits}

The real numbers are the complete ordered field: every bounded set has a least upper bound. Everything else in
analysis, limits, sums, derivatives and integrals, rests on this one property. This section defines suprema, the
limit of a sequence and Cauchy sequences, proves the monotone convergence theorem, and checks the limits of the
running examples in Sage.

### Suprema

Before limits can be discussed at all one needs to know which numbers exist, and the answer is encoded in a single
property of the real line. The definition below introduces the least upper bound of a set and states the
completeness axiom, the promise that every bounded set has one.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-supremum}
#### Supremum

A number $M$ is an **upper bound** of a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ if $s \leq M$ for every $s \in S$; the set is
**bounded above** if it has an upper bound. The **supremum** $\sup S$ is the least upper bound: an upper bound $M$
such that no $M' < M$ is an upper bound. The **completeness axiom** of the real numbers states that every non-empty
set bounded above has a supremum. The **infimum** $\inf S$, the greatest lower bound, is defined the same way with
the inequalities reversed, and $\inf S = -\sup(-S)$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first thing to see is that a least upper bound may or may not belong to the set, and that an unbounded set has
none at all. Sets with finitely many elements and intervals already show all three behaviours.

::: {#exm-sup-finite}
#### Finite sets and intervals

$\sup\{1, 4, 2\} = 4$, a maximum; $\sup [0, 1) = 1$, which is not an element of the set: a supremum need not be
attained. $\inf (0, \infty) = 0$ and the set $(0, \infty)$ has no supremum, being unbounded above.
:::

The next example is the set of values of a sequence, where the supremum is approached but never reached. Verifying
it requires the $\varepsilon$-argument that will reappear in the definition of a limit: nothing smaller than $1$
can be an upper bound.

::: {#exm-sup-sequence-set}
#### The set $\{1 - 1/n\}$

$S = \{1 - 1/n : n = 1, 2, \dots\} = \{0, \tfrac12, \tfrac23, \dots\}$ has $\sup S = 1$: every element is below
$1$, and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ the element with $n > 1/\varepsilon$ exceeds $1 - \varepsilon$, so nothing
smaller than $1$ is an upper bound (@exr-supremum-sage). This is the typical way a supremum is a limit.
:::

:::

Why should completeness be an axiom rather than a theorem? The third example answers by exhibiting a bounded set of
rationals with no rational least upper bound, so the property genuinely separates $\mathbb{R}$ from $\mathbb{Q}$.

::: {#exm-sup-rationals}
#### Why completeness is an axiom

The set $\{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q^2 < 2\}$ is bounded above in $\mathbb{Q}$ but has no least upper bound in
$\mathbb{Q}$, since $\sqrt2$ is irrational: the rationals are not complete. In $\mathbb{R}$ its supremum is
$\sqrt2$, and the completeness axiom is exactly what guarantees that such numbers exist.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Finding suprema and infima of concrete sets is the first skill to practise, including deciding whether they are
attained. The three sets below range from an alternating sequence to the values of $\sin n$, where the density of
the integers modulo $2\pi$ comes in.

::: {#exr-sup-examples}
#### Suprema and infima of explicit sets

Find $\sup$ and $\inf$ of $\{(-1)^n + 1/n : n \geq 1\}$, of $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 < 3\}$ and of
$\{\sin n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$, and say which are attained.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The first set is $\{0, \tfrac32, -\tfrac23, \tfrac54, -\tfrac45, \dots\}$: $\sup = \tfrac32$ (attained at $n = 2$)
and $\inf = -1$ (not attained, approached by the odd terms $-1 + 1/n$). The second is the interval $(-\sqrt3,
\sqrt3)$: $\sup = \sqrt3$, $\inf = -\sqrt3$, neither attained. The third has $\sup = 1$ and $\inf = -1$, neither
attained, since $\sin n = \pm1$ would need $n$ to be an odd multiple of $\pi/2$, which is irrational; the values
$\sin n$ come arbitrarily close to $\pm1$ because the integers modulo $2\pi$ are dense in $[0, 2\pi)$.
:::

The property that singled out $1$ as the supremum of $\{1 - 1/n\}$ is in fact a characterisation of the supremum,
and it is the form in which completeness is used in proofs. The second exercise asks for both directions of the
equivalence.

::: {#exr-sup-characterisation}
#### The $\varepsilon$-characterisation

Prove that $M$ is the supremum of a non-empty set $S$ if and only if $M$ is an upper bound and for every
$\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $s \in S$ with $s > M - \varepsilon$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $M = \sup S$ and some $\varepsilon > 0$ had no $s > M - \varepsilon$, then $M - \varepsilon$ would be an upper
bound smaller than $M$, contradicting leastness. Conversely, if $M$ is an upper bound with the $\varepsilon$
property, any $M' < M$ fails to be an upper bound: take $\varepsilon = M - M'$ and the corresponding $s > M'$. So
$M$ is the least upper bound.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Sequences.isLUB_iff_eps >}}

:::

### Limits of sequences

A sequence converges when its terms eventually stay as close to a number as one demands; the figure shows three
sequences entering a band of half-width $\varepsilon$ around their limits and never leaving it. The definition
below makes "eventually" and "as close as demanded" precise with the two quantifiers $\varepsilon$ and $N$, and
records the rules for combining limits.

![Three sequences and their limits: $1/n$ and $(-1)^n/n$ converge to $0$, $(1 + 1/n)^n$ converges to $e$; the
shaded bands have half-width $\varepsilon = 0.3$, and from $n = 4$ on every term lies inside its band. Generated by
`figures/sequence_limits.sage`.](figures/sequence_limits.svg){#fig-sequence-limits width=75%}

{{< interactive sequence_limits 460 >}}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sequence-limit}
#### Limit of a sequence

A **sequence** is a map $n \mapsto a_n$ from the positive integers to $\mathbb{R}$. It **converges** to the
**limit** $L$, written $a_n \to L$ or $\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = L$, if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$
such that $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \geq N$. A sequence with no limit **diverges**; $a_n \to \infty$ means
that for every $M$ there is an $N$ with $a_n > M$ for $n \geq N$. Limits are unique, and $a_n \to L$, $b_n \to M$
imply $a_n + b_n \to L + M$, $a_n b_n \to LM$ and $a_n / b_n \to L/M$ when $M \neq 0$ (the **limit rules**).
:::

Two of the facts quoted in the definition, uniqueness and the sum rule, have short proofs built on the triangle
inequality. The second exercise asks for them; the product and quotient rules follow the same pattern with one
extra estimate.

::: {#exr-limit-uniqueness}
#### Uniqueness of the limit and the sum rule

Prove that a sequence has at most one limit, and that $a_n \to L$ and $b_n \to M$ imply $a_n + b_n \to L + M$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $a_n \to L$ and $a_n \to L'$ with $L \neq L'$, take $\varepsilon = |L - L'|/2$; for large $n$ both $|a_n - L| <
\varepsilon$ and $|a_n - L'| < \varepsilon$, so $|L - L'| \leq |L - a_n| + |a_n - L'| < 2\varepsilon = |L - L'|$, a
contradiction. For the sum, given $\varepsilon$ choose $N$ such that $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon/2$ and $|b_n - M| <
\varepsilon/2$ for $n \geq N$ (the larger of the two $N$s); then $|(a_n + b_n) - (L + M)| \leq |a_n - L| + |b_n -
M| < \varepsilon$. The product and quotient rules are proved the same way with the estimate $|a_n b_n - LM| \leq
|a_n|\,|b_n - M| + |M|\,|a_n - L|$.
:::

### Cauchy sequences

The definition of a limit requires knowing the limit in advance, which is often exactly what one does not know. The
notion below tests convergence from the terms alone, by asking that they eventually cluster together, and
completeness guarantees that this is enough.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-cauchy-sequence}
#### Cauchy sequence

A sequence is a **Cauchy sequence** if its terms eventually stay close to each other: for every $\varepsilon > 0$
there is an $N$ such that $|a_m - a_n| < \varepsilon$ for all $m, n \geq N$. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy,
and in $\mathbb{R}$ every Cauchy sequence converges (the **Cauchy criterion**, equivalent to the completeness
axiom): convergence can be tested without knowing the limit.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `ra-convergent-cauchy-test.sage`; Test (oracle, 3 instances); record `KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Sequences.cauchy_converges.json`.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
One direction of the Cauchy criterion is elementary: terms close to a common limit are close to each other. The
first example gives the two-line proof and applies it to the running sequences.

::: {#exm-cauchy-convergent}
#### Convergent sequences are Cauchy

If $a_n \to L$, then for $m, n \geq N$ with $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon/2$, $|a_m - a_n| \leq |a_m - L| + |L - a_n| <
\varepsilon$. So $1/n$ and $(1 + 1/n)^n$ are Cauchy.
:::

The real use of the criterion is to prove convergence of a sequence whose limit is not yet known, by bounding the
distance between distant terms. The sums $s_n = \sum_{k \leq n} 1/k!$ are the standard case, with a geometric bound
on the tail.

::: {#exm-cauchy-factorial}
#### The partial sums of $\sum 1/k!$

$s_n = \sum_{k \leq n} 1/k!$ satisfies $|s_m - s_n| \leq 2/(n + 1)!$ for $m > n$, a tail bounded by a geometric
series (@exr-cauchy-decimal). The sequence is Cauchy, so it converges; its limit is $e$ again, and this is how $e$
is computed to many digits.
:::

The converse direction, that Cauchy sequences converge, is where completeness enters, and it fails in the
rationals. The third example makes this explicit with the decimal expansion of $\sqrt2$.

::: {#exm-cauchy-not-convergent-rationals}
#### Cauchy in $\mathbb{Q}$, not convergent in $\mathbb{Q}$

The decimal approximations $1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, \dots$ of $\sqrt2$ form a Cauchy sequence of rationals ($|a_m -
a_n| < 10^{-n}$) with no rational limit. The Cauchy criterion fails in $\mathbb{Q}$ and holds in $\mathbb{R}$: it is
a form of completeness (@exr-cauchy-rationals).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The partial sums of a geometric series are the simplest sequence whose Cauchy property can be checked by an
explicit bound on $|a_m - a_n|$. The first exercise asks for this bound and for the limit, anticipating the next
section.

::: {#exr-cauchy-geometric}
#### Geometric tails

Show that $a_n = \sum_{k=0}^n r^k$ is a Cauchy sequence for $|r| < 1$ by bounding $|a_m - a_n|$, and find its
limit.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $m > n$, $|a_m - a_n| = |r^{n+1} + \dots + r^m| \leq |r|^{n+1}(1 + |r| + \dots) = |r|^{n+1}/(1 - |r|)$, which is
below $\varepsilon$ for $n$ large since $|r|^{n+1} \to 0$. The limit is $1/(1 - r)$, from $a_n = (1 - r^{n+1})/(1 -
r)$ (@sec-series).
:::

The equivalence of the Cauchy criterion with completeness deserves a proof rather than a remark. The second
exercise asks for the failure in $\mathbb{Q}$ and for the derivation of the criterion from the supremum axiom,
through the suprema of tails.

::: {#exr-cauchy-rationals}
#### Completeness and the rationals

Explain why the sequence of decimal approximations of $\sqrt2$ shows that the Cauchy criterion fails in
$\mathbb{Q}$, and deduce that the completeness axiom implies the Cauchy criterion in $\mathbb{R}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The approximations $a_n$ are rational and Cauchy, and if they converged in $\mathbb{Q}$ their limit would also be
the real limit $\sqrt2$, which is irrational; so a Cauchy sequence of rationals need not converge in $\mathbb{Q}$.
In $\mathbb{R}$: a Cauchy sequence is bounded, so $L = \sup_n \inf_{m \geq n} a_m$ exists by completeness; for
$n \geq N(\varepsilon)$ all terms lie within $\varepsilon$ of $a_N$, hence so do the infima and their supremum $L$,
and $|a_n - L| < 2\varepsilon$: the sequence converges to $L$.
:::

### Monotone convergence

Monotone sequences are the case in which completeness gives convergence directly, with the supremum as the limit.
The theorem below is the first real theorem of the chapter, and its proof is the $\varepsilon$-characterisation of
the supremum applied once.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-monotone-convergence}
#### Monotone convergence theorem

An increasing sequence that is bounded above converges, to the supremum of its set of values; a decreasing sequence
bounded below converges to the infimum. *Proof.* Let $L = \sup_n a_n$, which exists by completeness. For
$\varepsilon > 0$ some $a_N > L - \varepsilon$ (@exr-sup-characterisation), and for $n \geq N$ monotonicity gives
$L - \varepsilon < a_N \leq a_n \leq L$, so $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (oracle, 3 instances); record `KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Sequences.monotone_convergence.json`; Test (oracle, 3 instances); record `KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Sequences.antitone_convergence.json`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Sequences.monotone_convergence >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Sequences.antitone_convergence >}}

**Sage.** Sage computes the limits of increasing bounded sequences and checks they bound the terms (the supremum); Sage computes the limits of decreasing bounded sequences and checks they are below the terms (the infimum).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The theorem applies at once to the sequence $1/n$, which decreases to its infimum. The first example records this,
showing how the theorem bypasses the $\varepsilon$-$N$ argument of @exm-limit-reciprocal.

::: {#exm-monotone-reciprocal}
#### Decreasing to the infimum

$1/n$ is decreasing and bounded below by $0$, so it converges to $\inf\{1/n\} = 0$: the theorem reproves
@exm-limit-reciprocal without an $\varepsilon$-$N$ argument.
:::

The theorem is most useful for recursively defined sequences, whose terms have no closed formula. Newton's
iteration for $\sqrt2$ is decreasing and bounded below, so it converges, and the recursion then identifies the
limit.

::: {#exm-monotone-sqrt2}
#### Newton's recursion for $\sqrt2$

$a_0 = 2$, $a_{n+1} = \tfrac12(a_n + 2/a_n)$ gives $2, 1.5, 1.4167, 1.41422, \dots$: decreasing (since $a_n^2 >
2$) and bounded below by $\sqrt2$, so convergent; the limit $L$ satisfies $L = \tfrac12(L + 2/L)$, that is, $L^2 =
2$ (@exr-monotone-sqrt2). The theorem gives existence of the limit, the recursion identifies it.
:::

The two estimates behind the convergence of $(1 + 1/n)^n$ are both binomial expansions, and the second exercise
works them out in full. The same computation yields the bound $e \leq 3$.

::: {#exr-monotone-e}
#### $(1 + 1/n)^n$ is increasing and bounded

Prove that $a_n = (1 + 1/n)^n$ is increasing and that $a_n < 3$ for all $n$, and conclude that it converges.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By the binomial theorem $a_n = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} n^{-k} = \sum_{k=0}^n \tfrac{1}{k!}\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(1 -
j/n)$. Each product increases with $n$ and $a_{n+1}$ has one more positive term, so $a_{n+1} > a_n$. Each product
is at most $1$, so $a_n \leq \sum_{k=0}^n 1/k! \leq 1 + \sum_{k=1}^n 2^{1-k} < 3$. By the monotone convergence
theorem $a_n$ converges, and the limit is by definition $e$; the same bound shows $e \leq 3$.
:::

A nested sequence of shrinking closed intervals pins down exactly one point; this is the form in which completeness
drives bisection arguments. The last exercise proves it from the monotone convergence theorem, applied to the two
sequences of endpoints.

::: {#exr-nested-intervals}
#### Nested intervals

Prove that a nested sequence of closed intervals $[a_n, b_n] \supseteq [a_{n+1}, b_{n+1}]$ with $b_n - a_n \to 0$
has exactly one common point.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$a_n$ is increasing and bounded above by $b_1$, $b_n$ decreasing and bounded below by $a_1$, so both converge, to
$a$ and $b$ with $a \leq b$; from $b_n - a_n \to 0$, $a = b$. The point $a$ lies in every interval ($a_n \leq a \leq
b_n$), and any other common point $c$ would satisfy $|c - a| \leq b_n - a_n$ for all $n$, forcing $c = a$. This is
the bisection argument behind the intermediate value theorem (@sec-continuity-differentiability).
:::

### Limits of the running sequences

The limits claimed for the running sequences are collected in one proposition, together with an explicit error
bound for the harmonic numbers. The list adds $n^{1/n} \to 1$ and the convergence of $H_n - \log n$ to
Euler's constant.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sequence-limits}
#### Limits of the running sequences

$1/n \to 0$, $(-1)^n/n \to 0$, $(1 + 1/n)^n \to e$, $n^{1/n} \to 1$, and the harmonic numbers satisfy $H_n - \log n
\to \gamma = 0.5772\ldots$ (Euler's constant), with $|H_{10^4} - \log 10^4 - \gamma| < 10^{-4}$.
:::

A symbolic limit is not a decimal approximation, and it helps to know what Sage does to obtain one. The first

::: {#exm-limits-sage}
#### How Sage finds a limit

`limit((1 + 1/n)^n, n=oo)` returns `e`: Sage rewrites the expression as $\exp(n\log(1 + 1/n))$ and expands the
logarithm, $n\log(1 + 1/n) = 1 - 1/(2n) + \dots \to 1$. The answer is symbolic, not a decimal approximation.
:::

The limit $n^{1/n} \to 1$ is less obvious than it looks, since base and exponent pull in opposite directions. A
binomial estimate settles it by hand, without logarithms.

::: {#exm-limits-nroot}
#### $n^{1/n} \to 1$ by hand

Write $n^{1/n} = 1 + h_n$ with $h_n \geq 0$; the binomial theorem gives $n = (1 + h_n)^n \geq \binom{n}{2} h_n^2$,
so $h_n^2 \leq 2/(n - 1) \to 0$ (@exr-limit-nroot).
:::

The harmonic numbers grow like $\log n$, and the difference converges to a constant with no known closed form. The
third example proves the convergence by monotone convergence and estimates how fast it takes place.

::: {#exm-limits-euler-constant}
#### Euler's constant

$H_n - \log n$ is decreasing and bounded below by $0$ (compare the sum with the integral of $1/x$,
@sec-riemann-integral), so it converges by @thm-monotone-convergence; the limit $\gamma$ has no known closed form.
At $n = 10^4$ the difference $H_n - \log n$ is within $10^{-4}$ of $\gamma$, and @exr-euler-constant shows the
error is close to $1/(2n)$.
:::

The binomial estimate used for $n^{1/n}$ extends to $a^{1/n}$ for every fixed $a > 0$, by squeezing between $1$ and
$n^{1/n}$. The first exercise asks for both limits, with the quotient rule handling $a < 1$.

::: {#exr-limit-nroot}
#### $n^{1/n}$ and $a^{1/n}$

Prove that $n^{1/n} \to 1$ and that $a^{1/n} \to 1$ for every $a > 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $n^{1/n}$ see @exm-limits-nroot: $0 \leq h_n \leq \sqrt{2/(n - 1)} \to 0$. For $a \geq 1$, $1 \leq a^{1/n} \leq
n^{1/n}$ once $n \geq a$, and the squeeze gives $a^{1/n} \to 1$; for $a < 1$ apply the result to $1/a$ and the
quotient rule.
:::

Squeezing a sequence between two others with the same limit was used informally for $n\sin(1/n)$ in @exr-limit-rules
 and deserves a statement and a proof. The second exercise supplies them and applies the theorem to two
trigonometric sequences, with Sage confirming.

::: {#exr-limit-squeeze}
#### The squeeze theorem

State and prove the squeeze theorem, apply it to $n\sin(1/n)$ and to $\sin(n)/n$, and check both limits in Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $a_n \leq b_n \leq c_n$ and $a_n, c_n \to L$, then $b_n \to L$: for $n \geq N$, $L - \varepsilon < a_n \leq b_n
\leq c_n < L + \varepsilon$. With $x = 1/n$: $\cos x \leq \sin x/x \leq 1$ for $0 < x \leq 1$ (from $x\cos x \leq
\sin x \leq x$), and $\cos(1/n) \to 1$, so $n\sin(1/n) \to 1$; and $-1/n \leq \sin(n)/n \leq 1/n$ gives $\sin(n)/n
\to 0$:

{{< sage exr-limit-squeeze >}}
:::

Convergence to $\gamma$ is slow, and the rate is worth measuring. The last exercise computes the differences $H_n -
\log n - \gamma$ and finds that they behave like $1/(2n)$, the first term of an asymptotic expansion.

::: {#exr-euler-constant}
#### The rate of convergence to $\gamma$

Compute $H_n - \log n$ for $n = 10, 10^2, 10^3, 10^4$, the differences to $\gamma$, and show numerically that they
behave like $1/(2n)$.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The products $2n\,(H_n - \log n - \gamma)$ approach $1$, consistent with the asymptotic expansion $H_n = \log n +
\gamma + 1/(2n) - 1/(12n^2) + \dots$ (an Euler-Maclaurin expansion, quoted without proof):

{{< sage exr-euler-constant >}}
:::

## Series {#sec-series}

A series is a sequence of partial sums; it converges when they do. This section defines series and absolute
convergence, states the comparison and ratio tests, introduces power series and their radius of convergence, and
evaluates the running series exactly in Sage: the geometric series, $\sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$, the exponential series
and the alternating harmonic series.

### Series and partial sums

An infinite sum has no meaning until one says which sequence is supposed to converge; the figure shows the partial
sums of three series, two settling down and one drifting off like $\log n$. The definition below identifies a
series with its sequence of partial sums and records the first necessary condition for convergence.

![Partial sums of three series: $\sum 2^{-n}$ converges to $1$, $\sum 1/n^2$ to $\pi^2/6$, and the harmonic series
diverges, its partial sums following $\log n + \gamma$ (dotted). Generated by
`figures/series_partial_sums.sage`.](figures/series_partial_sums.svg){#fig-series-partial-sums width=75%}

{{< interactive series_partial_sums 460 >}}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-series}
#### Series

The **series** $\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k$ with terms $a_k$ is the sequence of **partial sums** $s_n = a_1 + \dots +
a_n$. It **converges** to the **sum** $S$ if $s_n \to S$, and **diverges** otherwise. If the series converges then
$a_n = s_n - s_{n-1} \to 0$; the converse fails.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (oracle, 3 instances); record `KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.terms_tendsto_zero.json`; Test (oracle, 4 instances); record `KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.p_series.json`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.terms_tendsto_zero >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.p_series >}}

**Sage.** for convergent series (2^-k, 1/k², (-1/3)^k) Sage computes the sum (finite) and lim a_k = 0; Sage decides convergence of ∑ 1/k^p (Sage's sum, or its 'divergent' error) and compares with p > 1.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Powers of a fixed ratio form the one series whose partial sums have a closed form, which makes its convergence a
direct computation. The first example reads off the sum $1/(1 - r)$ and the condition $|r| < 1$.

::: {#exm-series-geometric}
#### The geometric series

$\sum_{k=0}^\infty r^k$ has $s_n = (1 - r^{n+1})/(1 - r)$ for $r \neq 1$, so it converges to $1/(1 - r)$ when $|r| <
1$ and diverges when $|r| \geq 1$: $\sum 2^{-k} = 2$, $\sum_{k \geq 1} 2^{-k} = 1$ (@fig-series-partial-sums, blue),
$\sum (-1/3)^k = 3/4$ (@exr-geometric-partial-sums).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.geom_partial >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.geometric_sums >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.geometric_diverges >}}

**Sage.** ∑_{k<N} r^k (1 - r) = 1 - r^N; Sage reports ∑ r^k divergent for |r| ≥ 1 (r = 1, -1, 2).
:::

The converse of the necessary condition fails, and the harmonic series is the standard witness: its terms tend to
zero but the sums grow without bound. The grouping argument below is Oresme's, from the fourteenth century.

::: {#exm-series-harmonic}
#### The harmonic series diverges

$\sum 1/k$ has terms tending to $0$ but diverges: grouping $1 + \tfrac12 + (\tfrac13 + \tfrac14) + (\tfrac15 + \dots +
\tfrac18) + \dots$, each group exceeds $\tfrac12$, so $s_{2^m} \geq 1 + m/2$. The partial sums grow like $\log n$
(@fig-series-partial-sums, red; @exr-series-necessary-condition).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.harmonic_two_pow >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.p_series >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.harmonic_log_bounds >}}

**Sage.** H_(2^m) ≥ 1 + m/2 in exact rational arithmetic; Sage decides convergence of ∑ 1/k^p (Sage's sum, or its 'divergent' error) and compares with p > 1; log(n + 1) ≤ H_n ≤ 1 + log n by 128-bit intervals.
:::

A series can converge without a closed form for its partial sums; one then proves convergence by bounding them and
identifies the sum by other means. The series $\sum 1/n^2$ is the showcase, with a telescoping bound and Euler's
value $\pi^2/6$.

::: {#exm-series-basel}
#### $\sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$

The partial sums increase and are bounded by $2$ (compare $1/k^2 \leq 1/(k(k-1)) = 1/(k-1) - 1/k$, a telescoping
sum), so the series converges by @thm-monotone-convergence; Euler found the sum $\pi^2/6$, and Sage returns it
exactly (@prp-series-values, @fig-series-partial-sums, green). The convergence is slow: the tail after $N$ terms is
about $1/N$ (@exr-basel-numeric).
:::

The closed form of the geometric partial sums is a one-line telescoping identity, and it explains the three
behaviours at $|r| < 1$, $r = 2$ and $r = -1$. The first exercise verifies it symbolically and evaluates several
cases in Sage.

::: {#exr-geometric-partial-sums}
#### The geometric series in closed form

Verify $s_n = \sum_{k=0}^n r^k = (1 - r^{n+1})/(1 - r)$ symbolically, evaluate the sum for $r = \tfrac12, -\tfrac13,
\tfrac{9}{10}$, and list the partial sums for $r = 2$ and $r = -1$.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(1 - r)s_n = (1 + r + \dots + r^n) - (r + \dots + r^{n+1}) = 1 - r^{n+1}$. For $|r| < 1$, $r^{n+1} \to 0$; for $r =
2$ the partial sums are $2^{n+1} - 1$, unbounded; for $r = -1$ they alternate between $1$ and $0$:

{{< sage exr-geometric-partial-sums >}}
:::

Telescoping is the other mechanism that gives partial sums in closed form, when each term is a difference $b_k -
b_{k+1}$. The second exercise has one convergent and one divergent telescoping series, the latter again with terms
tending to zero.

::: {#exr-telescoping}
#### Telescoping series

Evaluate $\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{k(k+1)}$ and $\sum_{k=1}^\infty \left(\sqrt{k+1} - \sqrt{k}\right)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{1}{k(k+1)} = \frac1k - \frac{1}{k+1}$, so $s_n = 1 - \frac{1}{n+1} \to 1$. The second has $s_n = \sqrt{n+1} -
1 \to \infty$: it diverges although its terms $\sqrt{k+1} - \sqrt k = 1/(\sqrt{k+1} + \sqrt k) \to 0$.
:::

The necessary condition $a_n \to 0$ and its failure as a sufficient condition are worth proving carefully. The last
exercise asks for the proof and for two divergent series with vanishing terms, one by grouping and one by
comparison.

::: {#exr-series-necessary-condition}
#### Terms tending to zero are not enough

Prove that $a_n \to 0$ is necessary for convergence, and give two divergent series with $a_n \to 0$, proving the
divergence of each.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $s_n \to S$ then $a_n = s_n - s_{n-1} \to S - S = 0$. The harmonic series diverges by the grouping of
@exm-series-harmonic, and $\sum 1/\sqrt k$ diverges because $1/\sqrt k \geq 1/k$ (comparison, @thm-convergence-tests).
Equivalently, $s_{2n} - s_n \geq n \cdot \frac{1}{2n} = \frac12$ for the harmonic series, so the partial sums are not
Cauchy.
:::

### Absolute convergence

Series with terms of both signs can converge because of cancellations, and such convergence is fragile. The
definition below separates the robust case, where the absolute values already converge, from the conditional one.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-absolute-convergence}
#### Absolute convergence

A series $\sum a_k$ **converges absolutely** if $\sum |a_k|$ converges. Absolute convergence implies convergence
(the partial sums are Cauchy, since $|s_m - s_n| \leq \sum_{k=n+1}^m |a_k|$), and the sum of an absolutely
convergent series does not depend on the order of its terms. A convergent series that does not converge absolutely
is **conditionally convergent**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `ra-abs-conv-conv-test.sage`; Test (oracle, 3 instances); record `KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.rearrangement_invariant.json`.

:::

Series whose terms are bounded in absolute value by a convergent positive series converge absolutely, and the
geometric series and the $p$-series are the usual comparison partners. The first example shows two such cases.

::: {#exm-absolute-geometric}
#### Geometric and $p$-series

$\sum (-\tfrac12)^k$ converges absolutely, since $\sum 2^{-k}$ converges; $\sum (-1)^k/k^2$ converges absolutely by
comparison with $\sum 1/k^2$. In general $\sum 1/k^p$ converges exactly for $p > 1$ (@exr-comparison-proof).
:::

The series $1 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 - \dots$ converges by the interlacing of its even and odd partial sums, yet its
absolute values form the divergent harmonic series. It is the basic example of conditional convergence, and its sum
is $\log 2$.

#### The alternating harmonic series

$\sum (-1)^{k+1}/k = 1 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 - \dots = \log 2$ converges (the partial sums with an even and an odd
number of terms are monotone and squeeze the limit; this is Leibniz's test) but not absolutely, the series of
absolute values being the harmonic series (@exr-absolute-alternating).
:::

What goes wrong with conditional convergence is that the sum depends on the order of the terms. The third example
rearranges the alternating harmonic series and halves its sum, and quotes Riemann's theorem that any sum can be
reached.

::: {#exm-absolute-rearrangement}
#### Rearranging a conditionally convergent series

Taking the terms of the alternating harmonic series in the order $1 - \tfrac12 - \tfrac14 + \tfrac13 - \tfrac16 -
\tfrac18 + \dots$ (one positive, two negative) gives the sum $\tfrac12\log 2$ instead of $\log 2$
(@exr-absolute-rearrangement); Riemann's rearrangement theorem states that a conditionally convergent series can be
rearranged to any sum. Absolutely convergent series have no such ambiguity.
:::

::: {#exr-absolute-alternating}
#### Leibniz's test on the alternating harmonic series

Show that $s_m - \log 2$ alternates in sign with $|s_m - \log 2| < 1/(m + 1)$, check it in Sage for $m = 10, 11,
100, 101$, and compare with the partial sums of the series of absolute values.

For an alternating series with $|a_k|$ decreasing to $0$, the even partial sums increase, the odd ones decrease,
and the two interlace: $s_{2n} \leq S \leq s_{2n+1}$, so the error after $m$ terms is at most the first omitted term
$1/(m + 1)$:

#### Absolute convergence implies convergence

Prove that $\sum |a_k| < \infty$ implies that $\sum a_k$ converges, and that $|\sum a_k| \leq \sum |a_k|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The partial sums $t_n = \sum_{k \leq n} |a_k|$ converge, so they are Cauchy; by the triangle inequality $|s_m - s_n|
= |\sum_{k=n+1}^m a_k| \leq \sum_{k=n+1}^m |a_k| = t_m - t_n$, so $s_n$ is Cauchy and converges
(@def-cauchy-sequence). Passing to the limit in $|s_n| \leq t_n$ gives the inequality for the sums.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The rearranged sum $\tfrac12\log 2$ can be computed exactly by regrouping the blocks, and watched numerically. The
last exercise does both and asks why an absolutely convergent series cannot be disturbed this way.

::: {#exr-absolute-rearrangement}
#### A rearrangement with a different sum

Compute the partial sums of the rearranged alternating harmonic series (one positive term, then two negative) after
$10, 100, 1000$ blocks and compare with $\tfrac12\log 2$; explain why absolutely convergent series are immune.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
After $b$ blocks the rearranged sum is $\sum_{j=1}^b \left(\tfrac{1}{2j-1} - \tfrac{1}{4j-2} - \tfrac{1}{4j}\right) =
\sum_j \left(\tfrac{1}{4j-2} - \tfrac{1}{4j}\right) = \tfrac12 \sum_j \left(\tfrac{1}{2j-1} - \tfrac{1}{2j}\right)
\to \tfrac12\log 2$. For an absolutely convergent series, every rearrangement's partial sums differ from the
original ones by at most a tail $\sum_{k > N}|a_k|$, which tends to zero:

{{< sage exr-absolute-rearrangement >}}
:::

### Convergence tests

Most series met in practice are not telescoping, and their convergence is decided by comparing them with a series
that is already understood. The theorem below gives the two workhorses, comparison with a dominating series and the
ratio test, whose proof reduces to a geometric comparison.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-convergence-tests}
#### Comparison and ratio tests

**Comparison test**: if $0 \leq a_k \leq b_k$ and $\sum b_k$ converges, then $\sum a_k$ converges; if $\sum a_k$
diverges, so does $\sum b_k$. **Ratio test**: if $a_k \neq 0$ and $|a_{k+1}/a_k| \to L$, the series $\sum a_k$
converges absolutely when $L < 1$ and diverges when $L > 1$; the test is inconclusive when $L = 1$. *Proof.* The
comparison test is the monotone convergence of the bounded partial sums. For the ratio test with $L < 1$, pick $L <
r < 1$; for $k \geq N$, $|a_{k+1}| \leq r|a_k|$, so $|a_k| \leq |a_N| r^{k-N}$ and the geometric series dominates;
for $L > 1$ the terms grow, so they do not tend to zero.
:::

#### $p$-series by comparison

For $p > 1$, $\sum 1/k^p$ converges by comparison with the condensed series $\sum 2^m \cdot 2^{-mp} = \sum

The convergence of $\sum 1/k^2$ is the case $p = 2$ (@exr-comparison-proof).

::: {#exr-comparison-proof}
#### The $p$-series

Prove that $\sum_{k \geq 1} 1/k^p$ converges if and only if $p > 1$, by Cauchy's condensation (grouping the terms
in blocks of length $2^m$).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The terms are decreasing, so the block $k = 2^m, \dots, 2^{m+1} - 1$ has sum between $2^m \cdot 2^{-(m+1)p}$ and
$2^m \cdot 2^{-mp}$. The series thus converges exactly when $\sum_m 2^{m(1-p)}$ does, a geometric series with ratio
$2^{1-p}$, which converges exactly when $p > 1$. For $p = 1$ this is the grouping of @exm-series-harmonic.
:::

### Power series

Series whose terms are powers of a variable define functions, and the most important functions of analysis arise
this way. The definition below introduces them and states the term-by-term operations, which the next section
justifies.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-power-series}
#### Power series

A **power series** centred at $x_0$ is a series of the form $\sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k (x - x_0)^k$ with
**coefficients** $c_k$; its sum, where it converges, is a function of $x$. Within its interval of convergence a
power series may be differentiated and integrated term by term, and the result is again a power series with the
same radius of convergence (@def-radius-of-convergence).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.TermwiseDerivative >}}

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The geometric series is the first power series, and differentiating or integrating it term by term produces new
series with known sums. The first example obtains $1/(1 - x)^2$ and $-\log(1 - x)$ this way.

#### The geometric series as a function

$\sum x^k = 1/(1 - x)$ for $|x| < 1$ (@exm-series-geometric). Differentiating term by term, $\sum k x^{k-1} = 1/(1 -
x)^2$, and integrating, $\sum x^{k+1}/(k + 1) = -\log(1 - x)$, both for $|x| < 1$ (@exr-power-series-geometric-derivative,
@exr-power-series-log).
:::

$e^x = \sum x^k/k!$, $\sin x = \sum (-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$, $\cos x = \sum (-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$ for all $x$; the
Taylor polynomials of @sec-continuity-differentiability are their partial sums (@exr-power-series-exp). Term-by-term
differentiation gives $(e^x)' = e^x$ and $(\sin x)' = \cos x$.

The binomial theorem extends to non-integer exponents as a power series, convergent for $|x| < 1$. The third
example states the series and shows the expansion of $\sqrt{1 + x}$ that gives the non-relativistic kinetic energy.

::: {#exm-power-binomial}
#### The binomial series

$(1 + x)^\alpha = \sum_k \binom{\alpha}{k} x^k$ for $|x| < 1$ and any real $\alpha$, with $\binom{\alpha}{k} =
\alpha(\alpha - 1)\cdots(\alpha - k + 1)/k!$; for $\alpha = -1$ it is the geometric series in $-x$, for $\alpha =
\tfrac12$ it gives $\sqrt{1 + x} = 1 + \tfrac{x}{2} - \tfrac{x^2}{8} + \dots$, the expansion behind the
non-relativistic limit $\sqrt{m^2 + p^2} \approx m + p^2/2m$.
:::

Term-by-term differentiation of $\sum x^k$ turns the sums $\sum k x^k$ and $\sum k^2 x^k$ into rational functions,
and evaluating at $x = \tfrac12$ gives exact values. The second exercise recovers the sum $6$ found numerically in

::: {#exr-power-series-geometric-derivative}
#### Differentiating the geometric series

Derive $\sum_{k \geq 1} k x^{k-1} = 1/(1 - x)^2$ and use it to evaluate $\sum_{k \geq 1} k/2^k$ and $\sum_{k \geq 1}
k^2/2^k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Term-by-term differentiation of $\sum x^k = 1/(1 - x)$ gives $\sum k x^{k-1} = 1/(1 - x)^2$; at $x = \tfrac12$,
$\sum k 2^{-k} = \tfrac12 \cdot 4 = 2$. Differentiating once more, $\sum k(k-1)x^{k-2} = 2/(1 - x)^3$, so $\sum k^2
x^k = x^2 \cdot 2/(1-x)^3 + x/(1-x)^2$, which at $x = \tfrac12$ gives $4 + 2 = 6$, the value found in
@exr-ratio-sage.
:::

Integrating the geometric series in $-x$ gives the series of $\log(1 + x)$, and at the endpoint $x = 1$ it becomes
the alternating harmonic series. The last exercise derives it and justifies the boundary value.

::: {#exr-power-series-log}
#### The series of the logarithm

Obtain the power series of $\log(1 + x)$ by integrating the geometric series in $-x$, verify it with Sage, and
evaluate it at $x = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{1}{1 + x} = \sum (-1)^k x^k$ for $|x| < 1$; integrating from $0$ to $x$, $\log(1 + x) = \sum_{k \geq 1}
(-1)^{k+1} x^k/k$. At $x = 1$ the series still converges (Leibniz) to $\log 2$, the alternating harmonic series of
@exm-absolute-alternating-harmonic (Abel's theorem justifies the boundary value):

{{< sage exr-power-series-log >}}
:::

### Radius of convergence

A power series converges on an interval centred at $x_0$, and the half-length of that interval is determined by the
coefficients alone. The definition below names it and gives two formulas for computing it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-radius-of-convergence}
#### Radius of convergence

The **radius of convergence** $R \in [0, \infty]$ of $\sum c_k (x - x_0)^k$ is the number such that the series
converges absolutely for $|x - x_0| < R$ and diverges for $|x - x_0| > R$; it is given by $R = 1/\limsup |c_k|^{1/k}$,
and by $R = \lim |c_k / c_{k+1}|$ when this limit exists. At the endpoints $|x - x_0| = R$ anything can happen.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (oracle, 4 instances); record `KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.radius_ratio.json`; Test (oracle, 4 instances); record `KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.CauchyHadamard.json`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.radius_ratio >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.CauchyHadamard >}}

**Sage.** Sage computes R = lim |c_k/c_(k+1)| and decides convergence inside and divergence outside (1/k, 1/k², 2^k); Sage computes ρ = lim |c_k|^(1/k) and the root test at x inside and outside 1/ρ.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The series met so far illustrate the three possibilities: a finite positive radius, an infinite one and zero. The
first example computes all of them from the ratio formula.

::: {#exm-radius-standard}
#### The standard series

$\sum x^k$ and $\sum x^k/k$ and $\sum x^k/k^2$ all have $R = 1$ (ratio $\to 1$); $\sum x^k/k!$ has $R = \infty$;
$\sum k!\,x^k$ has $R = 0$, converging only at $x = 0$ (@exr-radius-ratio).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (oracle, 4 instances); record `KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.radius_ratio.json`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Series.radius_ratio >}}

**Sage.** Sage computes R = lim |c_k/c_(k+1)| and decides convergence inside and divergence outside (1/k, 1/k², 2^k).
:::

The radius leaves the two endpoints undecided, and the series $\sum x^k$, $\sum x^k/k$ and $\sum x^k/k^2$ show
three different endpoint behaviours with the same radius $1$. The second example lists them.

::: {#exm-radius-boundary}
#### Behaviour at the endpoints

At $x = \pm1$: $\sum x^k$ diverges at both ends; $\sum x^k/k$ diverges at $1$ (harmonic) and converges at $-1$
(alternating harmonic); $\sum x^k/k^2$ converges absolutely at both. The radius says nothing about the endpoints
(@exr-radius-boundary).
:::

A function may be smooth on all of $\mathbb{R}$ and still have a power series of finite radius; the explanation
lies in the complex plane. The third example is $1/(1 + x^2)$, whose poles at $\pm i$ set the radius.

::: {#exm-radius-singularity}
#### The radius is the distance to the nearest singularity

$\frac{1}{1 + x^2} = \sum (-1)^k x^{2k}$ has $R = 1$ although the function is smooth on all of $\mathbb{R}$: the
obstruction is the pole at $x = \pm i$ in the complex plane, at distance $1$ from the centre
(@sec-complex-analysis). This is why power series are best understood over $\mathbb{C}$ (@exr-radius-complex).
:::

formula, by hand and in Sage.

\tfrac12, \infty$:

Determining the exact set of convergence requires the radius and a separate check of each endpoint. The second
exercise does this for three series, using the harmonic and alternating harmonic series at the ends.

::: {#exr-radius-boundary}
#### Endpoints of the interval of convergence

Determine the exact set of real $x$ for which $\sum x^k/k$ converges, and the same for $\sum x^k/k^2$ and $\sum
(-1)^k x^{2k}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sum x^k/k$: $R = 1$; at $x = 1$ harmonic (diverges), at $x = -1$ alternating harmonic (converges): the set is
$[-1, 1)$. $\sum x^k/k^2$: converges on $[-1, 1]$ (absolutely at both endpoints by the $p$-series with $p = 2$).
$\sum (-1)^k x^{2k}$: a geometric series in $-x^2$, converges exactly for $|x| < 1$, the open interval $(-1, 1)$.
:::

The distance-to-the-nearest-singularity rule gives the radius without computing a single coefficient. The last
exercise applies it to rational functions with real and complex poles, from two different centres.

::: {#exr-radius-complex}
#### Radius from a singularity

Without computing coefficients, find the radius of convergence at $x_0 = 0$ of the power series of $1/(1 + x^2)$,
of $1/(x - 2)$ and of $1/((x - 2)(x^2 + 9))$, and at $x_0 = 1$ for the last one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The radius is the distance from the centre to the nearest complex singularity (@sec-residues): $1$ (poles at $\pm
i$); $2$ (pole at $2$); $2$ at $x_0 = 0$ (poles at $2$ and $\pm 3i$, the nearest at distance $2$); at $x_0 = 1$ the
distances are $1$ and $\sqrt{10}$, so $R = 1$.
:::

### Sums of the running series

The values of the running series found in this section are collected in one proposition. The list includes the geometric series, the Basel sum, the harmonic divergence, the exponential series and
$\log 2$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-series-values}
#### Sums of the running series

$\sum_{n \geq 1} 2^{-n} = 1$, $\sum_{n \geq 1} 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$, the harmonic series diverges, $\sum_{n \geq 0}
x^n/n! = e^x$, and $\sum_{n \geq 1} (-1)^{n+1}/n = \log 2$.
:::

The remainder bound of the exponential series answers a practical question: how many terms give $e$ to a given
accuracy. The last exercise finds the number for ten digits and compares the bound with the actual error.

::: {#exr-exp-series-estimate}
#### How many terms for $e$ to ten digits?

Using the remainder bound of @exr-power-series-exp, find the smallest $m$ such that $\sum_{k \leq m} 1/k!$ agrees
with $e$ to within $10^{-10}$, and compare with the value $|s_{12} - e|$ computed in @exr-cauchy-decimal.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The remainder is below $1/m!$, and $1/13! = 1.6 \cdot 10^{-10}$, $1/14! = 1.1 \cdot 10^{-11}$, so $m = 14$ suffices
by the bound; the actual error is smaller (the bound overestimates by a factor close to $m$), and @exr-cauchy-decimal
found $|s_{12} - e| = 1.7 \cdot 10^{-10}$, already within $2 \cdot 10^{-10}$ at $m = 12$.
:::

## Continuity and differentiability {#sec-continuity-differentiability}

Limits of functions are limits of sequences of values; continuity says the limit is the value, differentiability
that the function is linear to first order. This section defines both, states the mean value theorem and Taylor's
theorem, and checks derivatives, Taylor polynomials and remainders in Sage, with $\sin x$ and $e^x$ as the running
examples.

### Limits of functions

What a function approaches near a point concerns the values nearby, not the value at the point itself. The
definition below is the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ version, its reformulation through sequences, and the one-sided and
infinite variants.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-function-limit}
#### Limit of a function

For $f$ defined near $a$ (not necessarily at $a$), $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means: for every $\varepsilon > 0$
there is a $\delta > 0$ such that $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ whenever $0 < |x - a| < \delta$. Equivalently, $f(x_n)
\to L$ for every sequence $x_n \to a$ with $x_n \neq a$. **One-sided limits** $\lim_{x \to a^\pm}$ restrict $x$ to one
side of $a$, and $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L$ means $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ for all $x$ beyond some $X$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Continuity.limit_eps_delta >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Continuity.limit_sequential >}}

:::

The function is undefined at $0$ but $\sin x / x \to 1$ as $x \to 0$: from $\cos x \leq \sin x / x \leq 1$ for $0 < |
x| \leq 1$ and the squeeze theorem (@exr-limit-squeeze). Likewise $(1 - \cos x)/x^2 \to \tfrac12$ and $(e^x -
1)/x \to 1$ (@exr-function-limits-sage).
:::

A limit can fail to exist in two different ways: the one-sided limits can disagree, or the function can oscillate
without settling. The second example has one case of each.

::: {#exm-flimit-one-sided}
#### A jump

$|x|/x$ equals $1$ for $x > 0$ and $-1$ for $x < 0$: the one-sided limits at $0$ are $\pm1$ and the two-sided limit
does not exist. The function $\sin(1/x)$ has no limit at $0$ either, oscillating between $-1$ and $1$ in every
neighbourhood of $0$.
:::

Limits at infinity compare the growth of the elementary functions, and the ordering exponentials, powers,
logarithms is used constantly. The third example lists the three basic cases.

::: {#exm-flimit-infinity}
#### Growth at infinity

$x e^{-x} \to 0$, $(\log x)/x \to 0$, $x^2/e^x \to 0$ as $x \to \infty$: exponentials beat powers and powers beat
logarithms. These limits control the convergence of improper integrals in @sec-riemann-integral.
:::

A proof from the definition requires producing $\delta$ from $\varepsilon$ explicitly, which for a polynomial means
a factorisation and a bound. The second exercise does this for $x^2$ at $2$.

::: {#exr-flimit-epsilon-delta}
#### An $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ proof

Prove from the definition that $\lim_{x \to 2} x^2 = 4$, giving $\delta$ in terms of $\varepsilon$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|x^2 - 4| = |x - 2|\,|x + 2|$. If $|x - 2| < 1$ then $|x + 2| < 5$, so $|x^2 - 4| < 5|x - 2|$; taking $\delta =
\min(1, \varepsilon/5)$ gives $|x^2 - 4| < \varepsilon$ whenever $0 < |x - 2| < \delta$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 4 instances); script `ra-sq-limit-delta-test.sage`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Continuity.sq_limit_delta >}}

**Sage.** |x - 2| < min(1, ε/5) ⇒ |x² - 4| < ε at sample ε, x.
:::

Characterising limits through sequences, as the definition does, turns questions about functions into questions
about sequences. The last exercise proves the equivalence and uses it to show that $\sin(1/x)$ has no limit at $0$.

::: {#exr-flimit-sequential}
#### The sequential characterisation

Prove that $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ if and only if $f(x_n) \to L$ for every sequence $x_n \to a$ with $x_n \neq
a$, and use it to show that $\sin(1/x)$ has no limit at $0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition holds and $x_n \to a$, then for $n$ large $0 < |x_n - a| < \delta$, so
$|f(x_n) - L| < \varepsilon$. Conversely, if the condition fails for some $\varepsilon$, then for every $\delta =
1/n$ there is $x_n$ with $0 < |x_n - a| < 1/n$ and $|f(x_n) - L| \geq \varepsilon$: a sequence $x_n \to a$ with
$f(x_n) \not\to L$. For $\sin(1/x)$ take $x_n = 1/(2\pi n)$ (values $0$) and $x'_n = 1/(2\pi n + \pi/2)$ (values
$1$): two sequences tending to $0$ with different limits of values, so no limit exists.
:::

### Continuity

Continuity at a point means that the limit equals the value, and continuity on an interval has strong consequences.
The definition below records the algebraic rules and the two theorems on closed bounded intervals.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-continuity}
#### Continuous function

$f$ is **continuous at** $a$ if $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$, and **continuous** on a set if it is continuous at
every point of it. Sums, products, quotients with non-zero denominator and compositions of continuous functions
are continuous; polynomials, $\exp$, $\sin$, $\cos$ are continuous on $\mathbb{R}$, $\log$ on $(0, \infty)$. A
continuous function on a closed bounded interval $[a, b]$ is bounded, attains its maximum and minimum
(**extreme value theorem**) and takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ (**intermediate value theorem**).
:::

The intermediate value theorem is how the existence of roots is proved without a formula, and bisection makes the
proof constructive. The third example locates $\sqrt[3]2$ this way.

::: {#exm-continuity-ivt}
#### A root by the intermediate value theorem

$f(x) = x^3 - 2$ has $f(1) = -1 < 0 < f(2) = 6$, so it has a root in $(1, 2)$, namely $\sqrt[3]{2}$; bisecting the
interval repeatedly (@exr-nested-intervals) locates it to any precision. This is how the existence of roots and
inverse functions is proved.
:::

Two facts about continuous functions, composition and the fixed-point property on $[0, 1]$, are proved from the
sequential characterisation and the intermediate value theorem. The second exercise asks for both.

::: {#exr-continuity-composition}
#### Composition and the intermediate value theorem

Prove that the composition of continuous functions is continuous, and that a continuous $f : [0, 1] \to [0, 1]$ has
a fixed point.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $x_n \to a$ then $f(x_n) \to f(a)$ by continuity of $f$, and then $g(f(x_n)) \to g(f(a))$ by continuity of $g$
at $f(a)$: the sequential characterisation gives continuity of $g \circ f$. For the fixed point, $h(x) = f(x) - x$
is continuous with $h(0) = f(0) \geq 0$ and $h(1) = f(1) - 1 \leq 0$; by the intermediate value theorem $h$
vanishes somewhere, and there $f(x) = x$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The extreme value theorem needs a closed and bounded interval, and dropping either hypothesis breaks it. The last
exercise asks for counterexamples on $(0, 1]$ and $[0, \infty)$ and for the hypothesis that fails in each.

::: {#exr-continuity-extreme}
#### Why closed and bounded

Give continuous functions on $(0, 1]$ and on $[0, \infty)$ that are unbounded or do not attain their supremum, and
explain which hypothesis of the extreme value theorem fails in each case.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$1/x$ on $(0, 1]$ is continuous and unbounded (the interval is not closed at $0$); $x/(1 + x)$ on $[0, \infty)$ is
bounded by $1$ and never attains it (the interval is not bounded); $x$ on $(0, 1)$ attains neither its supremum
$1$ nor its infimum $0$. The theorem needs both closedness and boundedness, that is, compactness
(@sec-compact-connected).
:::

### The derivative

Differentiability means that a function is well approximated by a straight line near a point; the figure shows the
next step of the same idea, the Taylor polynomials of $\sin x$ matching the function on longer and longer
intervals. The definition below introduces the derivative as the slope of that line and lists the rules for
computing it.

![Taylor polynomials $T_1, T_3, T_5, T_7$ of $\sin x$ at $0$: each adds one term of the power series and matches
the function on a longer interval; the remainder of $T_7$ is bounded by $|x|^9/9!$. Generated by
`figures/taylor_sin.sage`.](figures/taylor_sin.svg){#fig-taylor-sin width=75%}

{{< interactive taylor_sin 460 >}}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-derivative}
#### Derivative

$f$ is **differentiable at** $a$ if the **difference quotient** $(f(a + h) - f(a))/h$ has a limit as $h \to 0$; the
limit is the **derivative** $f'(a) = \frac{df}{dx}(a)$, the slope of the tangent line, and $f(a + h) = f(a) + f'(a)h +
o(h)$. A differentiable function is continuous. The derivative obeys the **sum, product, quotient and chain
rules**: $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$, $(f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g^2$, $(g \circ f)' = (g' \circ f)\,f'$, and $(f^{-1})'(y) =
1/f'(x)$ at $y = f(x)$ when $f'(x) \neq 0$.
:::

nowhere.

The product and chain rules have short proofs from the definition, the key step being an add-and-subtract trick.
The second exercise asks for the product rule in full and the chain rule in outline.

::: {#exr-derivative-product-rule}
#### Proving the product and chain rules

Prove $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$ from the definition, and sketch the proof of the chain rule.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f(a + h)g(a + h) - f(a)g(a) = [f(a + h) - f(a)]\,g(a + h) + f(a)\,[g(a + h) - g(a)]$; divide by $h$ and let $h \to
0$, using the continuity of $g$ at $a$ for $g(a + h) \to g(a)$. For the chain rule write $f(a + h) = f(a) + k$ with
$k = f'(a)h + o(h)$; then $g(f(a + h)) - g(f(a)) = g'(f(a))\,k + o(k) = g'(f(a)) f'(a) h + o(h)$, so the derivative
is $g'(f(a)) f'(a)$.
:::

The inverse function rule produces the derivatives of $\arcsin$ and $\arctan$ from those of $\sin$ and $\tan$. The
last exercise derives both, the second being the integrand of @exr-improper-integrals-sage.

::: {#exr-derivative-inverse}
#### The derivative of an inverse function

Derive $(\arcsin x)' = 1/\sqrt{1 - x^2}$ and $(\arctan x)' = 1/(1 + x^2)$ from the inverse function rule.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $y = \arcsin x$, $x = \sin y$ and $(\arcsin)'(x) = 1/\cos y = 1/\sqrt{1 - \sin^2 y} = 1/\sqrt{1 - x^2}$ (the
positive root since $\cos y > 0$ on $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$). With $y = \arctan x$, $(\arctan)'(x) = 1/(1 + \tan^2 y) =
1/(1 + x^2)$, the integrand whose integral over $\mathbb{R}$ is $\pi$ (@exr-improper-integrals-sage).
:::

### The mean value theorem

The derivative at a point controls the function near it; the theorem below makes this global, relating the
increment over an interval to the derivative at some interior point. It is proved from the extreme value theorem
through Rolle's theorem, and its consequences are the ones used throughout the book.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-mean-value}
#### Mean value theorem

If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, there is a $c \in (a, b)$ with $f(b) - f(a) =
f'(c)(b - a)$. *Proof.* The function $g(x) = f(x) - f(a) - \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}(x - a)$ vanishes at $a$ and $b$;
by the extreme value theorem it attains a maximum or minimum at an interior point $c$ (unless it is constant, when
any $c$ works), and there $g'(c) = 0$ (Rolle's theorem), which is the claim. Consequences: $f' = 0$ on an interval
forces $f$ constant, $f' > 0$ forces $f$ increasing, and $|f'| \leq M$ gives $|f(x) - f(y)| \leq M|x - y|$.
:::

The consequence used most is that two functions whose derivatives agree differ by a constant. The second example
states it and explains why it makes antiderivatives essentially unique.

::: {#exm-mvt-constant}
#### Functions with the same derivative

If $f' = g'$ on an interval then $(f - g)' = 0$, so $f - g$ is constant: antiderivatives are unique up to a
constant. This is what makes the fundamental theorem of calculus (@thm-fundamental-theorem) a statement about a
single function $F$.
:::

Bounding the derivative bounds the increment, which is the mean value theorem used as an inequality. The third
example applies this to $\sin$ and $\exp$ and points to the error estimates that follow.

::: {#exm-mvt-lipschitz}
#### Bounding a difference

$|\sin x - \sin y| \leq |x - y|$ because $|\cos| \leq 1$; $|e^x - e^y| \leq e^{\max(x,y)}|x - y|$. Such bounds, with
the derivative controlling the increment, are the basis of the error estimates of numerical analysis and of
Taylor's theorem.
:::

The sign of the derivative determines monotonicity, and this gives a clean method for proving inequalities. The
second exercise proves the monotonicity statement and the inequality $e^x > 1 + x$.

::: {#exr-mvt-monotone}
#### Derivatives and monotonicity

Prove that $f' > 0$ on an interval implies that $f$ is strictly increasing, and use it to show that $e^x > 1 + x$
for $x \neq 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $x < y$ the mean value theorem gives $f(y) - f(x) = f'(c)(y - x) > 0$. Let $g(x) = e^x - 1 - x$: $g'(x) = e^x -
1$ is negative for $x < 0$ and positive for $x > 0$, so $g$ decreases to $g(0) = 0$ and then increases; hence $g(x) >
0$ for $x \neq 0$. The bound $e^x \geq 1 + x$ is used in @exr-monotone-e's companion estimate $\log(1 + 1/n) \leq
1/n$.
:::

Rolle's theorem, the special case with equal endpoint values, counts roots: between two roots of $f$ lies a root of
$f'$. The last exercise uses it for a cubic and for the general bound on the number of roots of a polynomial.

::: {#exr-mvt-rolle}
#### Rolle's theorem and roots

Use Rolle's theorem to show that $x^3 + x - 1$ has exactly one real root, and that a polynomial of degree $n$ has
at most $n$ real roots.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f(0) = -1 < 0 < f(1) = 1$ gives a root by the intermediate value theorem; two roots would give, by Rolle, a zero
of $f'(x) = 3x^2 + 1 > 0$ between them, which is impossible. Inductively, if a degree-$n$ polynomial had $n + 1$
roots, its derivative (degree $n - 1$) would have $n$ roots between them, contradicting the induction hypothesis.
:::

### Taylor's theorem

The tangent line is the first-order approximation; higher-order approximations by polynomials come with an explicit
remainder. The theorem below gives the Taylor polynomial and the Lagrange form of the error, which is what makes
the approximation usable.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-taylor}
#### Taylor's theorem

If $f$ has $n + 1$ continuous derivatives near $a$, then $f(a + h) = T_n(h) + R_n(h)$ with the **Taylor
polynomial** $T_n(h) = \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!} h^k$ and the **Lagrange remainder** $R_n(h) =
\frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!} h^{n+1}$ for some $c$ between $a$ and $a + h$; in particular $|R_n(h)| \leq
\frac{M}{(n+1)!}|h|^{n+1}$ if $|f^{(n+1)}| \leq M$ on the interval. *Proof.* Apply the mean value theorem (in Cauchy's
form) to $f - T_n$ and $h^{n+1}$ repeatedly, $n + 1$ times.
:::

$T_7(x) = x - x^3/6 + x^5/120 - x^7/5040$, and since $|\sin^{(9)}| \leq 1$ the remainder is at most $|x|^9/9!$
(@fig-taylor-sin, @prp-derivative-values). On $[-\pi, \pi]$ this is below $0.083$; on $[-1, 1]$ below $3 \cdot
10^{-6}$. As $n \to \infty$ the polynomials converge to $\sin x$ for every $x$: the power series of
@exm-power-exponential.
:::

Taylor series can converge to the wrong function, so smoothness is weaker than being given by a power series. The
third example is the standard one, $e^{-1/x^2}$ with all derivatives zero at the origin.

::: {#exm-taylor-non-analytic}
#### A Taylor series that misses the function

$f(x) = e^{-1/x^2}$ for $x \neq 0$, $f(0) = 0$, has all derivatives zero at $0$: its Taylor series is identically
$0$ and converges everywhere, but to the wrong function. Smoothness does not imply analyticity; over $\mathbb{C}$
it does (@sec-holomorphic).
:::

The remainder bound tells which degree guarantees a prescribed accuracy on a given interval. The second exercise
works this out for $\sin x$ on two intervals and two tolerances.

::: {#exr-taylor-remainder-bound}
#### How many terms?

How many terms of the Taylor series of $\sin x$ at $0$ are needed to guarantee an error below $10^{-6}$ on $[-\pi,
\pi]$? Below $10^{-10}$ on $[-1, 1]$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The remainder after $T_{2m-1}$ is at most $\pi^{2m+1}/(2m+1)!$ on $[-\pi, \pi]$: $m = 8$ gives $\pi^{17}/17! = 8.0
\cdot 10^{-7}$, so $T_{15}$ (eight non-zero terms) suffices. On $[-1, 1]$ the bound is $1/(2m+1)!$, and $1/15! =
7.6 \cdot 10^{-13}$, so $T_{13}$ (seven terms) gives $10^{-10}$; already $T_{11}$ gives $1/13! = 1.6 \cdot
10^{-10}$, just above the target.
:::

The second-order Taylor expansion decides whether a critical point is a minimum or a maximum. The last exercise
proves the second-derivative test and applies it to the double-well potential of spontaneous symmetry breaking.

::: {#exr-taylor-second-derivative}
#### Second-order conditions

Use Taylor's theorem to show that if $f'(a) = 0$ and $f''(a) > 0$ then $f$ has a strict local minimum at $a$, and
apply it to the potential $V(\phi) = \tfrac14(\phi^2 - 1)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f(a + h) = f(a) + \tfrac12 f''(c) h^2$ with $c$ between $a$ and $a + h$; by continuity $f''(c) > 0$ for small $h$,
so $f(a + h) > f(a)$ for $0 < |h|$ small. For $V$: $V'(\phi) = \phi(\phi^2 - 1)$ vanishes at $0, \pm1$, and $V''(\phi)
= 3\phi^2 - 1$ is $-1$ at $0$ (a local maximum) and $2$ at $\pm1$ (minima). The two minima at $\phi = \pm1$ are the
degenerate vacua of the symmetry-breaking potential of @sec-ssb.

::: {#exr-derivative-higher}
#### Higher derivatives

Find a formula for the $n$-th derivative of $x^2 e^x$ and prove it by induction.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(x^2 e^x)^{(n)} = (x^2 + 2nx + n(n-1))e^x$: true for $n = 0$; differentiating, $(2x + 2n)e^x + (x^2 + 2nx +
n(n-1))e^x = (x^2 + 2(n+1)x + (n+1)n)e^x$. Sage's `diff(x^2*exp(x), x, 2)` gives $(x^2 + 4x + 2)e^x$, the case $n
= 2$ (@exr-derivative-sage).
:::

The symmetry of a function is reflected in its Taylor series: even functions have only even powers, odd functions
only odd ones. The second exercise proves this and checks it on sine and cosine.

::: {#exr-taylor-cos-even}
#### Even and odd functions

Show that the Taylor series at $0$ of an even function has only even powers and that of an odd function only odd
powers, and verify on $\cos x$ and $\sin x$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Differentiating $f(-x) = f(x)$ $k$ times gives $(-1)^k f^{(k)}(-x) = f^{(k)}(x)$, so at $0$ the odd derivatives
vanish; for odd $f$ the even ones vanish. $\cos$ has $\cos^{(k)}(0) = 1, 0, -1, 0, \dots$ and $\sin^{(k)}(0) = 0, 1,
0, -1, \dots$, giving the series of @exm-power-exponential.
:::

The series of $\arctan$ at $x = 1$ gives $\pi/4$, but very slowly; Machin's formula uses small arguments to speed
it up. The last exercise estimates the number of terms needed in each case.

::: {#exr-taylor-pi-estimate}
#### $\pi$ from $\arctan$

Using $\arctan x = \sum (-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$ for $|x| \leq 1$, estimate how many terms give $\pi/4 = \arctan 1$
to three decimals, and why Machin's formula $\pi/4 = 4\arctan\tfrac15 - \arctan\tfrac1{239}$ converges so much
faster.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At $x = 1$ the series is alternating with terms $1/(2k+1)$, so the error after $k$ terms is about $1/(2k+3)$: three
decimals need $k \approx 500$. In Machin's formula the arguments are small, and the terms $(1/5)^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$
shrink geometrically: eight terms give ten decimals. The series of $\arctan$ is the integrated geometric series in
$-x^2$ (@exm-power-geometric).
:::

## The Riemann integral {#sec-riemann-integral}

The integral measures the area under a graph as a limit of sums of rectangles; the fundamental theorem of calculus
turns it into the inverse of differentiation. This section defines the Riemann integral and antiderivatives,
proves the fundamental theorem, treats improper integrals, and computes the Gaussian integral $\int e^{-x^2}dx =
\sqrt\pi$, the integral behind every Gaussian probability and every free field theory.

### The integral as a limit of sums

The area under a graph is approximated from below and from above by rectangles, and the figure shows both
approximations for $x^2$ on $[0, 1]$ closing in as the subintervals shrink. The definition below makes this the
definition of the integral, and lists the functions for which the two approximations meet and the basic properties
of the result.

![Lower (blue) and upper (red) Riemann sums of $x^2$ on $[0, 1]$ with $n = 4$ and $n = 16$ subintervals; both
converge to the integral $\tfrac13$, and their difference is $1/n$. Generated by
`figures/riemann_sums.sage`.](figures/riemann_sums.svg){#fig-riemann-sums width=85%}

{{< interactive riemann_sums 440 >}}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-riemann-integral}
#### Riemann integral

For $f$ bounded on $[a, b]$ and a **partition** $a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b$, the **lower** and **upper sums**
are $L = \sum_k m_k (x_k - x_{k-1})$ and $U = \sum_k M_k (x_k - x_{k-1})$ with $m_k, M_k$ the infimum and supremum
of $f$ on $[x_{k-1}, x_k]$. $f$ is **Riemann integrable** if $\sup L = \inf U$ over all partitions, and the common
value is the **integral** $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$. Continuous functions, and bounded functions with finitely many
discontinuities, are integrable; the integral is linear, monotone ($f \leq g$ implies $\int f \leq \int g$) and
additive over intervals, and $\int_a^b f = -\int_b^a f$.
:::

Integrability is a matter of the upper and lower sums approaching each other, and for monotone functions this
follows from a telescoping estimate. The second example gives it and explains the exact gap $1/n$ of the first.

::: {#exm-integral-monotone}
#### Monotone functions are integrable

For $f$ increasing, $U - L = \sum_k (f(x_k) - f(x_{k-1}))(x_k - x_{k-1}) \leq (f(b) - f(a))\max_k (x_k - x_{k-1})$,
which tends to $0$ as the partition is refined: this is why $U - L = 1/n$ exactly for $x^2$ on $[0, 1]$.
:::

Not every bounded function is integrable: if every subinterval contains values near $0$ and near $1$, the sums
never meet. The indicator function of the rationals is the standard example, and it motivates the Lebesgue
integral.

::: {#exm-integral-dirichlet}
#### A function that is not integrable

The indicator function of the rationals on $[0, 1]$ has $m_k = 0$ and $M_k = 1$ on every subinterval, so $\sup L = 0
< 1 = \inf U$: it is not Riemann integrable. The Lebesgue integral of @sec-hilbert-spaces assigns it the value $0$.
:::

For a linear function the midpoint rule is exact, and seeing why is a first lesson in numerical integration. The
second exercise computes the lower, upper and midpoint sums for $\int_0^1 x\,dx$.

::: {#exr-integral-linear}
#### Integrating a linear function

Compute $\int_0^1 x\,dx$ directly from lower and upper sums with $n$ equal subintervals, and show that the
midpoint sum is exact for every $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Lower sum $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (k/n)/n = (n-1)/(2n)$, upper sum $(n+1)/(2n)$, both tending to $\tfrac12$. The midpoint
sum $\sum_k ((k + \tfrac12)/n)/n = \tfrac12$ exactly, because the midpoint rule integrates linear functions
exactly on each subinterval.
:::

The definition's claim that functions with finitely many discontinuities are integrable rests on enclosing each
jump in a small subinterval. The last exercise proves this for step functions and for a single jump.

::: {#exr-integral-step}
#### Step functions and integrability

Show that a step function (constant on finitely many intervals) is integrable, and that a bounded function with a
single jump discontinuity is integrable.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For a step function choose partitions containing the jump points; then $U - L$ is at most the sum of the jumps
times the lengths of the subintervals containing them, which can be made arbitrarily small. For a bounded $f$ with
one jump at $c$ and bound $M$, enclose $c$ in a subinterval of length $\delta$; its contribution to $U - L$ is at
most $2M\delta$, and on the rest $f$ is continuous, hence integrable. The argument extends to finitely many jumps.
:::

### Antiderivatives

Computing integrals from Riemann sums is impractical; the practical route is through functions whose derivative is
the integrand. The definition below introduces them and the two techniques that produce them, both derivative rules
read backwards.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-antiderivative}
#### Antiderivative

An **antiderivative** (or **primitive**) of $f$ on an interval is a function $F$ with $F' = f$; it is unique up to
an additive constant (@exm-mvt-constant), and $\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C$ denotes the family. The techniques
**integration by parts**, $\int f g' = fg - \int f' g$, and **substitution**, $\int f(g(x)) g'(x)\,dx = \int f(u)\,du$,
are the product and chain rules read backwards.
:::

**Lean.**

Every derivative formula is an antiderivative formula in reverse, and the list below is the derivative table of the
previous section turned around. The first example records it.

::: {#exm-antiderivative-table}
#### The basic table

$\int x^n\,dx = x^{n+1}/(n+1)$ for $n \neq -1$, $\int dx/x = \log|x|$, $\int e^x\,dx = e^x$, $\int \sin x\,dx = -\cos
x$, $\int dx/(1 + x^2) = \arctan x$, $\int dx/\sqrt{1 - x^2} = \arcsin x$: each line is a derivative of
@sec-continuity-differentiability read backwards.
:::

Moving a derivative from one factor to the other trades one integral for another, and is the tool for products with
polynomials or logarithms. The second example has two standard cases and the factorial integral obtained by
repeating the step.

::: {#exm-antiderivative-parts}
#### Integration by parts

$\int x e^x\,dx = x e^x - \int e^x\,dx = (x - 1)e^x$, and $\int \log x\,dx = x\log x - x$ (take $g' = 1$). Repeated
parts give $\int_0^\infty x^n e^{-x}\,dx = n!$ (@exr-improper-integrals-sage), the integral defining the Gamma
function of @sec-analytic-continuation.

Antiderivatives are found by pattern recognition: parts, substitution or partial fractions, depending on the
integrand. The first exercise has one of each type.

::: {#exr-antiderivative-table}
#### Finding antiderivatives

Find antiderivatives of $x\cos x$, $\log x / x$, $\tan x$ and $1/(x^2 - 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By parts: $x\sin x + \cos x$. Substitution $u = \log x$: $\tfrac12(\log x)^2$. $\tan x = \sin x/\cos x$,
substitution $u = \cos x$: $-\log|\cos x|$. Partial fractions $\frac{1}{x^2 - 1} = \tfrac12\left(\frac{1}{x - 1} -
\frac{1}{x + 1}\right)$: $\tfrac12\log\left|\frac{x - 1}{x + 1}\right|$.
:::

Reduction formulas lower the exponent in an integral step by step, and the one for $\sin^n$ leads to Wallis's
product. The second exercise derives it by parts and evaluates two cases.

::: {#exr-antiderivative-reduction}
#### A reduction formula

Show that $I_n = \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^n x\,dx$ satisfies $I_n = \frac{n-1}{n} I_{n-2}$, and compute $I_4$ and $I_5$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Integrate by parts with $f = \sin^{n-1}x$, $g' = \sin x$: $I_n = [-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x]_0^{\pi/2} + (n-1)\int
\sin^{n-2}x\cos^2 x\,dx = (n-1)(I_{n-2} - I_n)$, so $n I_n = (n-1)I_{n-2}$. With $I_0 = \pi/2$ and $I_1 = 1$: $I_4 =
\tfrac34 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac\pi2 = 3\pi/16$ and $I_5 = \tfrac45 \cdot \tfrac23 = 8/15$. Wallis's product for
$\pi$ follows from $I_{2n}/I_{2n+1} \to 1$.
:::

In a definite integral the substitution changes the limits too, and forgetting this is the usual mistake. The last
exercise has two substitutions with the limits tracked.

::: {#exr-antiderivative-substitution}
#### Substitution in definite integrals

Evaluate $\int_0^1 x\sqrt{1 - x^2}\,dx$ and $\int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\cos x}{1 + \sin^2 x}\,dx$ by substitution, taking
care of the limits.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$u = 1 - x^2$, $du = -2x\,dx$, limits $1 \to 0$: $\tfrac12\int_0^1 \sqrt u\,du = \tfrac13$. $u = \sin x$, $du = \cos
x\,dx$, limits $0 \to 1$: $\int_0^1 du/(1 + u^2) = \arctan 1 = \pi/4$.
:::

### The fundamental theorem

The two halves of the section, the integral as a limit of sums and the antiderivative, are connected by the
fundamental theorem, which is why both are called integration. The theorem below states both directions and proves
them from continuity and the mean value theorem.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-fundamental-theorem}
#### Fundamental theorem of calculus

If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, then $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ is differentiable with $F' = f$ (every continuous
function has an antiderivative), and for any antiderivative $G$ of $f$, $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = G(b) - G(a)$. *Proof.*
$F(x + h) - F(x) = \int_x^{x+h} f(t)\,dt$ lies between $h\min f$ and $h\max f$ over $[x, x + h]$, and both bounds
tend to $h f(x)$ by continuity, so $F'(x) = f(x)$. Then $G - F$ is constant (@exm-mvt-constant), and $G(b) - G(a) =
F(b) - F(a) = F(b)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (oracle, 4 instances); record `KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Integral.fundamental_theorem.json`.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Integral.fundamental_theorem >}}

**Sage.** Sage's ∫ₐᵇ f = G(b) - G(a) and d/dx ∫ₐˣ f = f for sample f, G.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is the simplest use of the theorem: an antiderivative is known, and the integral is a difference
of its values. The area under one arch of the sine comes out as exactly $2$.

::: {#exm-ftc-sin}
#### $\int_0^\pi \sin x\,dx = 2$

$G = -\cos x$ is an antiderivative, so the integral is $-\cos\pi + \cos 0 = 2$ (@prp-integral-values): the area under
one arch of the sine is exactly $2$.
:::

The other direction of the theorem produces antiderivatives even when no formula exists. The second example
differentiates the error-function integral and recovers the Gaussian.

::: {#exm-ftc-erf}
#### Differentiating an integral

$F(x) = \int_0^x e^{-t^2}dt$ has $F'(x) = e^{-x^2}$ although $F$ has no elementary formula; in terms of the error
function, $F(x) = \frac{\sqrt\pi}{2}\operatorname{erf}(x)$ (@exr-fundamental-theorem-sage). The theorem produces
antiderivatives even when no formula exists.
:::

The logarithm can be defined as an integral, and the theorem shows that this definition agrees with the usual one.
The third example also connects the integral with the harmonic numbers.

::: {#exm-ftc-log}
#### The logarithm as an integral

$\log x = \int_1^x dt/t$ for $x > 0$: the right side is differentiable with derivative $1/x$ and vanishes at $1$, so
it equals $\log x$ by uniqueness of antiderivatives. The comparison of $\sum 1/k$ with this integral is what shows
$H_n - \log n$ bounded in @exm-limits-euler-constant.
:::

When both limits of an integral depend on $x$ the chain rule enters; when the integrand does too, more care is
needed. The second exercise has one case of each, the latter being a solution formula for $y'' = f$.

::: {#exr-ftc-leibniz}
#### Differentiating with variable limits

Compute $\frac{d}{dx}\int_{x}^{x^2} e^{-t^2}dt$ and $\frac{d}{dx}\int_0^x (x - t) f(t)\,dt$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By the fundamental theorem and the chain rule, $\frac{d}{dx}\int_{u(x)}^{v(x)} g(t)\,dt = g(v)v' - g(u)u'$: here
$2x e^{-x^4} - e^{-x^2}$. For the second, expand $\int_0^x (x - t)f(t)\,dt = x\int_0^x f - \int_0^x t f(t)\,dt$;
differentiating gives $\int_0^x f(t)\,dt + x f(x) - x f(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$, and differentiating again gives
$f(x)$: this integral is the solution of $y'' = f$ with $y(0) = y'(0) = 0$ (@sec-odes).
:::
